questions.question: What is the virtual DOM?
options: A faster, alternative browser rendering engine
A lightweight in-memory object tree describing what the UI should look like
A cache of previously rendered HTML strings
A separate thread that runs alongside the main JS thread
questions.explanation: It's plain JavaScript objects (produced by createElement/JSX), not a browser feature — React diffs these objects instead of touching the real DOM on every change.

questions.question: When the element type at a given position changes (e.g. `<div>` becomes `<span>`), what does React do?
options: Patches the existing DOM node's tag name in place
Tears down the old subtree and builds a new one from scratch
Throws an error requiring a full page reload
Ignores the change until the next render
questions.explanation: Reconciliation assumes different element types produce fundamentally different trees, so React discards and rebuilds rather than trying to patch across types.

questions.question: Why does using the array index as a `key` cause bugs when a list can be reordered or filtered?
options: Each list item's internal state stays attached to its position (index) rather than following the logical item, so state can appear to jump to the wrong row
It only affects performance, never correctness
questions.explanation: React matches by key across renders; with index keys, an item that moved from index 2 to index 0 is treated as 'the item that was at index 0 changed', dragging along any state (like an input's value) tied to that position.

questions.question: What capability does the Fiber architecture provide that the older recursive renderer did not?
options: The ability to skip virtual DOM diffing entirely
The ability to pause, prioritize, and resume rendering work instead of blocking the main thread until a render finishes
questions.explanation: Fiber breaks rendering into interruptible units of work, which is also the foundation that makes concurrent features like useTransition possible.
